clue.text: Signs of dissent with the things dancers may do

blocks.note: first meaning: divisions within a party or group
second meaning: the floor move with legs stretched flat in opposite directions

explanation.surface: Rebellious dancers make their disagreement known through their moves.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both rifts in a group and the gymnastic leg-stretch that dancers perform on the floor.

clue.text: Keep going in a jam

definitions.note: a noun phrase: what goes into a jam jar

blocks.note: first meaning: to maintain or save something
second meaning: fruit cooked into a jam or conserve

explanation.surface: Advice to persevere when you are in a tight spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep going' reads as one phrase meaning persevere, but it splits: 'Keep' is the verb, and the rest describes the fruit stuff spread on toast.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep something is to save it from decay, and a fruit conserve or jam is also called by this name.

clue.text: Start formally to admit

blocks.note: first meaning: to begin something officially
second meaning: to bring a newcomer into a society with a ceremony

explanation.surface: A formal opening at which someone confesses something.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to set a process going officially and to induct a new member into a club or secret society.

clue.text: Tourist, a great deal with a prophet

blocks.note: informal: 'a sight better' means a great deal better
a seer foresees the future

explanation.surface: A tourist getting a bargain, accompanied by a fortune-teller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A great deal' looks like a bargain, but it is the informal intensifier 'a sight', as in 'a sight too clever'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tourist is a visitor who goes round looking at famous places and attractions on holiday.

clue.text: Fielders cut off? Twaddle

blocks.note: in cricket the slips are fielders standing beside the wicketkeeper
to lop is to cut off, as a branch

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator dismissing as nonsense the idea that fielders were cut off.
explanation.walkthrough: Slips are cricket fielders posted close behind the batsman on the off side.
explanation.definitionFit: Slipslop is an old word for watery food and, by extension, feeble nonsense talk or writing.

clue.text: England bowler who put th.' game first

definitions.text: England bowler who put th.' game first

blocks.note: surface reading: a cricketer selected to bowl for the national team
setter's reading: the Elizabethan admiral who, by legend, finished his game of bowls on Plymouth Hoe before sailing against the Armada

explanation.surface: A dedicated England cricket bowler who always prioritised the sport.
explanation.walkthrough: The bowler here plays lawn bowls, not cricket: the famous story has the admiral insist on finishing his game before facing the Spanish fleet in 1588.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tudor sea captain is remembered for playing bowls calmly while the Spanish Armada approached English shores.

clue.text: Treat, of course

blocks.note: first meaning: to subject material to a series of operations
second meaning: a series of actions or a progression

explanation.surface: Offering someone a treat, naturally, as a matter of course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' reads as an idiom, but 'of' is only the joint and 'course' is a noun meaning a series of steps.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means handle by a set method; as a noun it means a series of steps or a natural progression.

clue.text: Find congenial — and sensible also

blocks.note: to like someone is to find them agreeable
wise means showing good judgment

explanation.surface: Someone who finds a person pleasant and also level-headed.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means in the same way or as well, adding a further item to what has been said.

clue.text: So sorry a character, Rowe's fair Calista

definitions.note: the character's title role, from the play's name

blocks.note: first meaning: feeling regret for wrongdoing
second meaning: Calista is the heroine of Nicholas Rowe's 1703 tragedy The Fair ...

explanation.surface: An apology to a woman named Calista, a character in a play by Rowe.
explanation.walkthrough: Nicholas Rowe was an English playwright and Poet Laureate; his tragedy's title names its heroine Calista by this word.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone deeply sorry for their sins is contrite, and Calista is the title figure of Rowe's play The Fair Penitent.

clue.text: See big possibilities about return for investor

indicators.note: possibilities are different ways things could turn out, so the letters may be ordered another way
to return is to go back, so the word just before it is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: taken as written, ready for rearranging
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A financial adviser pointing out big opportunities for a good return to someone with money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Investor' and 'return' suggest finance, but to invest a town is an old military term for surrounding it.
explanation.definitionFit: To invest a fortress is to surround it with troops, so an investor in this military sense lays siege to it.

clue.text: Bare suggestion for Hamlet's suicide weapon

definitions.text: Bare suggestion for Hamlet's suicide weapon

blocks.note: surface reading: a mere hint or proposal, with nothing more to it
setter's reading: in the 'To be or not to be' speech Hamlet says one might end it all 'with a bare' small dagger

explanation.surface: Someone tentatively proposes what Hamlet might use to kill himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bare' is lifted from Shakespeare's line 'When he himself might his quietus make / With a bare bodkin'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet's soliloquy names a short pointed dagger as the simple instrument a man could take his own life with.

clue.text: Agencies have a high place for the middle man

blocks.note: media are channels or agencies through which things are done or communicated
a tor is a rocky hilltop, as on Dartmoor in south-west England

explanation.surface: Organisations want to give a top position to a go-between.
explanation.definitionFit: A go-between who negotiates between two disagreeing parties stands in the middle, helping them reach agreement.

clue.text: Bird whose cry returns to it

indicators.note: something that returns comes back the way it went, so the word before is read backwards

blocks.note: to cry is to weep
taken as written; 'to' joins it on

explanation.surface: A bird whose call echoes back to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cry' suggests a bird call, which is fitting since the bird's name imitates its call, but here it means shed tears.
explanation.definitionFit: The lapwing, a plover of fields and moors, is also called by this name, which imitates its call.

clue.text: Obligations all round — think of old maids

indicators.note: all round means surrounding entirely, so one set of letters wraps another

blocks.note: ties are bonds or obligations
ween is an archaic verb meaning think or suppose

explanation.surface: Remember the old spinsters, with duties surrounding them on all sides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old maids' suggests spinsters, but here it is servants: a tweeny was a between-maid helping both cook and housemaid.
explanation.definitionFit: In Victorian and Edwardian households a between-maid assisting both kitchen and housemaid staff was called a tweeny.

clue.text: Earthquake spot in east — disturbance one per cent

indicators.note: a disturbance throws things out of order, so the following letters get jumbled

blocks.note: E is the compass abbreviation
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A news report on an earthquake in the east that disturbed only one per cent of the region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disturbance' fits the quake surface, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The point on the ground directly above where a tremor starts is the centre of the shaking.

clue.text: We beg for his sake

blocks.note: surface reading: someone pleading on behalf of another person
setter's reading: the exasperated plea 'for ___'s sake', named after a man

explanation.surface: People pleading on behalf of a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation 'For Pete's sake!' is a mild substitute for invoking God, used when begging someone to stop.
explanation.definitionFit: The man named in the exasperated exclamation 'for his sake' is a euphemism standing in for a holier name.

clue.text: Times, following what they do in the corridors

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the first word's letters are placed second

blocks.note: people walking along a narrow hallway go by one another
ages are long periods of time

explanation.surface: A note about what people get up to in office hallways at certain times.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition doubles as part of the wordplay: in hallways, people go by one another.
explanation.definitionFit: Corridors are long narrow ways connecting rooms inside a building, and the plural noun names them.

clue.text: Rolling-stock item was first to be submitted

blocks.note: a truck is an open railway wagon
to have led is to have been in front

explanation.surface: A railway wagon was the first one to be handed in.
explanation.walkthrough: Rolling stock is the general term for railway vehicles, and in Britain an open goods wagon is called a truck.
explanation.definitionFit: To truckle is to give in servilely to someone more powerful, so the past tense means yielded or submitted.

clue.text: Where to go for curtains

blocks.note: surface reading: the shop or department selling window drapes
setter's reading: curtains is slang for death, and the idiom for dying names a compass direction

explanation.surface: Shopping advice on where to buy new drapes.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'go west' is an old idiom for to die or be destroyed, and 'curtains' is slang for the end or death.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'go west' means to perish, so this is the direction you head when it is curtains for you.

clue.text: Watts — his ruler is flapping

blocks.note: W is the symbol for watts
taken as written
a king is a ruler

explanation.surface: A man named Watts reporting that his monarch is in a panic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watts' looks like a surname, but it is the unit, abbreviated W.
explanation.definitionFit: Whisking means flicking or sweeping something about with quick light movements, as a tail swats flies.

clue.text: Pride's remedy, swallowed by son of the preacher

indicators.note: what is swallowed ends up inside, so one word goes into the other

blocks.note: taken as written
Pride's Purge of 1648 was Colonel Thomas Pride's removal of opponents from the English Parliament

explanation.surface: A cure for vanity is swallowed by the minister's son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pride' looks like the sin, but it is the Civil War colonel whose purge of Parliament is a famous historical episode.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Haddon Spurgeon was a celebrated Victorian Baptist minister, known as the Prince of Preachers in London.

clue.text: Big drinker gets round the bar — somewhat weak

indicators.note: to get round something is to encircle it, so one word wraps the other

blocks.note: a heavy drinker 'drinks like a fish'
a rail is a bar

explanation.surface: A heavy drinker propped against the pub counter, a bit unsteady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' and 'big drinker' suggest a pub, but the bar is a rod and the drinker is a creature of the water.
explanation.definitionFit: The -ish suffix softens frail, which means delicate or lacking strength, giving 'a little feeble'.

clue.text: Offer it turns out fine

indicators.note: something that turns out is rearranged into a new form, so the letters are reshaped

blocks.note: taken as written, ready for rearranging

explanation.surface: An offer that proves to be fine after all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' reads as an adjective meaning all right, but it is the noun: a penalty.
explanation.definitionFit: A forfeit is a penalty paid for an error or offence, as a fine is a sum paid as punishment.

clue.text: Obtain reliable safe

blocks.note: first meaning: to get hold of, as in securing a deal
second meaning: firmly fixed and dependable
third meaning: protected from danger

explanation.surface: Get hold of a dependable strongbox.
explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings, not two: 'safe' looks like a noun for a strongbox, but it is a third adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to get or acquire; as an adjective it means dependable and also protected from harm.

clue.text: Cup-holders? They can tire one

blocks.note: first meaning: kitchen sideboards with shelves and hooks for crockery
second meaning: tire is an old word for attire, so these are people who clothe someone, like a theatre's wardrobe assistants

explanation.surface: Sports trophy winners complaining that the effort exhausts them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tire' looks like exhaust, but it is short for attire: to dress someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Kitchen cabinets display cups on hooks, and theatre assistants who clothe actors share the same name.

clue.text: Sportsman to beat again in return

indicators.note: in return means coming back the other way, so the words before are read backwards

blocks.note: re- is the prefix meaning again
to flog is to beat

explanation.surface: A sportsman seeking revenge, wanting to beat his rival again in the return match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' suggests a return fixture, but it is the reversal signal for the whole of the beat-again verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A golfer is a player of the club-and-ball game, so he is one kind of sportsman.

clue.text: End it, at a possibility achieved

indicators.note: a possibility is one of several ways things might go, so the letters may take another order

blocks.note: taken as written, ready for rearranging

explanation.surface: Ending something as a possibility that was achieved.
explanation.definitionFit: To attain a goal is to reach or accomplish it, so the past form means reached or accomplished.

clue.text: After directions, case becomes calmer

definitions.note: a noun here: something that calms

indicators.note: after means coming later, so the second word's letters go at the end

blocks.note: south and east, two compass points
the dative is a grammatical case, used for an indirect object

explanation.surface: Following instructions, a legal case becomes less heated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' suggests law, but it is grammar; 'calmer' looks like a comparative adjective but is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A sedative is a drug that soothes nerves and induces sleep, so it acts as something that quietens a patient.

clue.text: What “moves in predestinate grooves”

blocks.note: surface reading: a quotation from a limerick about a man complaining he is a mere creature of fate
setter's reading: a machine running on rails follows a track fixed in advance

explanation.surface: A puzzle about who or what follows a fate laid down in advance.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from a limerick by Maurice Evan Hare, whose speaker laments being 'not a bus, not a bus, but a tram'.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway locomotive runs on fixed rails, so its route is set in advance just as fate seems predestined.
